## Results

The 21 participants retained after exclusions (Methods) contributed 997 valid first fixations out of 1008 trials: 11 LTR participants (523 trials) and 10 RTL participants (474 trials). The 11 dropped trials split into 7 first fixations faster than 80 ms and 4 trials with no fixation in either area of interest. All results below use the first fixation computed from FPOG, the tracker classified measure used throughout preprocessing. A sensitivity check against raw gaze samples instead of classified fixations, reported in Methods, leaves every conclusion here unchanged.

### Left/right and up/down bias by group

@fig-orientation-bias and @tbl-orientation-bias give the pooled proportion of trials on which each group's first fixation went left, right, up, or down, with hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals. `physical_side` and `physical_vert` are the same clock-hour-derived columns from Preprocessing, each skipping the one arrangement that carries no information for that axis:

```python
def pooled_orientation_table(df, axis_col, positive_label, negative_label):
    rows, subj_rows = [], []
    for group, g in df.dropna(subset=[axis_col]).groupby("group"):
        per_subj = [(subj, (sg[axis_col] == positive_label).astype(float).values)
                    for subj, sg in g.groupby("subject_nr")]
        arrays = [a for _, a in per_subj]
        p_pos, lo_pos, hi_pos = hierarchical_bootstrap_ci(arrays)
        rows.append(dict(group=group, direction=positive_label, n_subjects=len(arrays),
                          n_trials=len(g), p=p_pos, ci_lo=lo_pos, ci_hi=hi_pos))
        rows.append(dict(group=group, direction=negative_label, n_subjects=len(arrays),
                          n_trials=len(g), p=1 - p_pos, ci_lo=1 - hi_pos, ci_hi=1 - lo_pos))
        for subj, a in per_subj:
            subj_rows.append(dict(group=group, subject_nr=subj,
                                   direction=positive_label, p=a.mean()))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), pd.DataFrame(subj_rows)


group_lr, subj_lr = pooled_orientation_table(df_valid_fpog, "physical_side", "right", "left")
group_ud, subj_ud = pooled_orientation_table(df_valid_fpog, "physical_vert", "up", "down")
group_dir = pd.concat([group_lr, group_ud], ignore_index=True)
```

| Group | Direction | P(first fixation) | 95% CI |
|:------|:----------|-------------------:|:-------|
| LTR | left  | 71.8% | [64.2%, 79.5%] |
| LTR | right | 28.2% | [20.5%, 35.8%] |
| LTR | up    | 72.6% | [62.5%, 81.5%] |
| LTR | down  | 27.4% | [18.5%, 37.5%] |
| RTL | left  | 49.0% | [37.4%, 60.5%] |
| RTL | right | 51.0% | [39.5%, 62.6%] |
| RTL | up    | 83.4% | [76.9%, 89.3%] |
| RTL | down  | 16.6% | [10.7%, 23.1%] |

: Pooled first-fixation direction by group (FPOG-based), with hierarchical bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. {#tbl-orientation-bias}

![First-fixation direction by reading group. Bars are the group mean (hierarchical bootstrap CI); dots are individual subject means; the dashed line marks chance.](../images/results/group_orientation_bias_fpog.png){#fig-orientation-bias width="85%"}

Both groups fixate up well above chance. On left/right the two groups part company. LTR's leftward bias of 71.8% sits inside the 60% to 93% range reported for comparable paradigms in the literature reviewed in the Introduction, and its interval is comfortably clear of chance. RTL's proportions land almost exactly on 50%, with a marginal lean to the right (51.0%) and an interval, [39.5%, 62.6%], that spans chance with room to spare. In other words the RTL group as a whole has no measurable horizontal preference on this measure, which is the direction the hypotheses predicted but a weaker result than a reversal would be. The two intervals overlap, so the raw proportions alone cannot settle whether the groups differ; the regression below is the test that can.

The up/down contrast runs the other way. RTL's upward bias of 83.4% is larger than LTR's 72.6%, and RTL's interval is the tightest of the four. Nothing in the hypotheses anticipated a group difference on the vertical axis.

### Clock-face profile

@fig-clock-face breaks the same bias down by all twelve clock positions rather than collapsing to left/right and up/down. Each trial contributes to the two hours actually presented in its arrangement, so every hour's estimate is conditioned on having been on screen at all:

```python
rows = []
for _, r in df_valid_fpog.dropna(subset=["fixated_clock"]).iterrows():
    for h in r["arrangement"]:
        rows.append(dict(group=r["group"], subject_nr=r["subject_nr"], hour=int(h),
                          fixated=float(r["fixated_clock"] == h)))
clock_long = pd.DataFrame(rows)

subj_clock = (clock_long.groupby(["group", "subject_nr", "hour"])["fixated"]
              .agg(["mean", "count"]).reset_index())
group_clock = (subj_clock.groupby(["group", "hour"])["mean"]
               .mean().reset_index(name="p"))  # mean of subject means
```

![P(first fixation on this clock position, given it was presented), by group. Thick lines are group means; thin lines are individual subjects.](../images/results/clock_face_bias_fpog.png){#fig-clock-face width="80%"}

Both groups favour the top of the clock and avoid the bottom. Every hour from 10 to 1 sits above chance in both groups, and no hour from 4 to 7 does in either. The upper half is where the two profiles separate. LTR peaks on the left flank, at 11 o'clock (91.7%) and 9 o'clock (87.5%), while RTL peaks at 12 (97.5%) and spills to the right, with hours 1 and 2 at 83.4% and 79.5%. The pair of hours on the horizontal meridian makes the same point most directly, since neither carries any vertical component: LTR fixates 9 o'clock first on 87.5% of trials and 3 o'clock on 12.5%, whereas RTL splits them 51.2% to 48.8%.

Two individual hours diverge more than the pooled contrasts suggest, although each hour rests on about eight trials per subject and is correspondingly noisier. Hour 2, in the upper right, is RTL's largest lead anywhere on the clock: 79.5% against LTR's 35.2%. Hour 6, at the bottom, is the most extreme point on the plot for either group. LTR still fixates it first on 13.6% of trials, against 2 of 79 trials for RTL. Because opposite hours are two views of the same choice, the mirrored hours (8 and 12) tell the same story rather than adding to it.

### Individual-subject bias vectors

@fig-quadrant plots each subject as a single point: horizontal bias (P(right) minus P(left)) against vertical bias (P(up) minus P(down)), each rescaled from a 0 to 1 proportion to a -1 to 1 bias so that 0 means no preference:

```python
subj_rows = []
for (group, subj), g in df_valid_fpog.groupby(["group", "subject_nr"]):
    px = (g["physical_side"].dropna() == "right").astype(float).values
    py = (g["physical_vert"].dropna() == "up").astype(float).values
    subj_rows.append(dict(group=group, subject_nr=subj,
                           x=2 * px.mean() - 1, y=2 * py.mean() - 1))
quad_subj = pd.DataFrame(subj_rows)

group_rows = []
for group, g in df_valid_fpog.groupby("group"):
    side_arrays = [(sg["physical_side"].dropna() == "right").astype(float).values
                   for _, sg in g.groupby("subject_nr")]
    vert_arrays = [(sg["physical_vert"].dropna() == "up").astype(float).values
                   for _, sg in g.groupby("subject_nr")]
    px, px_lo, px_hi = hierarchical_bootstrap_ci(side_arrays)
    py, py_lo, py_hi = hierarchical_bootstrap_ci(vert_arrays)
    group_rows.append(dict(group=group, x=2 * px - 1, y=2 * py - 1,
                            x_ci_lo=2 * px_lo - 1, x_ci_hi=2 * px_hi - 1,
                            y_ci_lo=2 * py_lo - 1, y_ci_hi=2 * py_hi - 1))
quad_group = pd.DataFrame(group_rows)
```

![First-fixation bias as a 2-D vector. Diamonds are group means with hierarchical bootstrap CIs; dots are individual subjects.](../images/results/quadrant_bias_fpog.png){#fig-quadrant width="75%"}

The LTR mean falls in the up-left quadrant (x = -0.44, y = 0.45) with both intervals clear of zero, so LTR is reliably biased up and to the left as a group. The RTL mean sits just across the vertical axis at x = 0.02, y = 0.67: reliably upward, since its vertical interval excludes zero, but horizontally indistinguishable from no preference, with an interval of [-0.21, 0.26] straddling zero. That matches @tbl-orientation-bias.

The individual points are worth reading alongside the means. Five subjects lean rightward, and all five are RTL: subjects 54 (x = 0.10), 65 (0.20), 111 (0.23), 64 (0.45) and 66 (0.65), the largest rightward lean in the sample. No LTR subject does; the most extreme in that group is subject 108 at x = -0.90. On the vertical axis the picture is more uniform. Every RTL subject has a positive value, between 0.40 and 0.85, and only two participants anywhere in the sample fall below zero: LTR subjects 101 (-0.05) and 106 (-0.11), both close enough to zero to read as no vertical preference rather than a downward one.

### A single test of the group difference

The proportions above answer four separate questions (left/right and up/down, for each group) rather than the one question of primary interest: do LTR and RTL differ once each arrangement's own baseline preference is accounted for? Methods describes a logistic regression built for exactly this: the log odds of fixating the clockwise-numbered stimulus in each pair (`img_right`, the one-to-six o'clock member), as a function of arrangement (six levels) and group:

```python
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

df_bt = df_valid_fpog.copy()
df_bt["y_right"] = (df_bt["fpog_first_fix_direction"] == "right").astype(int)
df_bt["arrangement_str"] = df_bt["arrangement"].astype(str)

bt_model = smf.logit("y_right ~ C(arrangement_str) + C(group)", data=df_bt).fit(
    disp=0, cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df_bt["subject_nr"]})
```

The model converges cleanly (n = 997) and standard errors are clustered by subject, since trials from the same subject are not independent, the same reason the proportions above use a hierarchical bootstrap.

Arrangement drives most of the fit. Relative to the baseline arrangement, 10 and 4 o'clock, the two arrangements without an upper-left stimulus (7 and 1 o'clock; 8 and 2 o'clock) sharply raise the odds of fixating the clockwise-numbered member of the pair (b = 2.54, p < .001; b = 1.63, p < .001). Those are also two of the three arrangements with the largest slow latency tails below. The remaining two non-baseline arrangements (11 and 5 o'clock; 12 and 6 o'clock) lower the odds instead (b = -0.74, p = .005; b = -1.15, p = .022), and only 9 and 3 o'clock does not differ from baseline (p = .173).

Group is significant in the predicted direction: the RTL coefficient is b = 1.08 (cluster SE = 0.41, p = .009). Fit without clustering the same coefficient reaches p < .001, which overstates the case: that version treats all 997 trials as independent observations when there are only 21 subjects behind them, so it is not the one reported. The clustered result is the one that matters, and it says the groups differ once each arrangement's own pull is taken out, even though RTL's raw left/right proportion on its own sits at chance.

An arrangement by group interaction, which would give each arrangement its own group comparison instead of one pooled test, was checked and not used:

```python
inter_model = smf.logit("y_right ~ C(arrangement_str) * C(group)", data=df_bt).fit(disp=0)
# converges, but in the (12, 6)/RTL cell only 2 of 79 trials went to
# the clockwise member, which leaves that comparison on very little
```

Every cell is populated, so the model converges, but with 10 RTL subjects spread across twelve arrangement-by-group cells and no clustered version of it fitted, its per-arrangement estimates are not solid enough to report next to the additive model.

### The same test, one axis at a time

The outcome in that model, "fixated the one-to-six o'clock member," is a horizontal contrast in the 9-3 arrangement and a vertical one in 12-6, so the group coefficient mixes the reading-direction effect with the vertical difference seen above. Refitting the same model to each axis separately keeps the two apart:

```python
def group_effect(df, outcome_col, positive, label, with_arrangement=True):
    d = df.dropna(subset=[outcome_col]).copy()
    d["y"] = (d[outcome_col] == positive).astype(int)
    d["arrangement_str"] = d["arrangement"].astype(str)
    formula = "y ~ C(arrangement_str) + C(group)" if with_arrangement else "y ~ C(group)"
    return smf.logit(formula, data=d).fit(disp=0, cov_type="cluster",
                                           cov_kwds={"groups": d["subject_nr"]})


horizontal_only = df_valid_fpog[df_valid_fpog["arrangement"].astype(str) == "(9, 3)"]
group_effect(df_valid_fpog, "physical_side", "right", ...)          # drops 12-6
group_effect(df_valid_fpog, "physical_vert", "up", ...)             # drops 9-3
group_effect(horizontal_only, "physical_side", "right", ..., with_arrangement=False)
```

| Outcome | Trials | b (RTL) | SE | p |
|:--------|-------:|--------:|---:|--:|
| clockwise member, all six arrangements | 997 | +1.08 | 0.41 | .009 |
| P(right), 12-6 dropped | 832 | +1.32 | 0.38 | .001 |
| P(up), 9-3 dropped | 829 | +0.70 | 0.34 | .037 |
| P(right) in 9-3 alone | 168 | +1.90 | 0.65 | .004 |

: The group effect split by axis. All four models cluster standard errors by subject. {#tbl-axis-split}

Both axes carry a group difference, and the horizontal one is the stronger of the two (b = 1.32 against b = 0.70). The cleanest version of it is the last row: in the 9-3 arrangement, where the choice is purely left against right and no vertical preference can contribute, LTR fixates the right-hand stimulus first on 12.5% of trials and RTL on 48.8%. That is the reading-direction prediction in its most direct form, and it holds even though RTL's pooled left/right proportion across all arrangements sits at chance.

### First-fixation latency by arrangement

@fig-latency shows the share of trials with a first fixation slower than 2000 ms, separately by arrangement and group; 2000 ms is a descriptive boundary at the valley of the bimodal latency distribution, not an exclusion criterion:

```python
SLOW_MS = 2000

lat = df_valid_fpog.dropna(subset=["fpog_first_fix_rt_ms"]).copy()
lat["arrangement_lbl"] = lat["arrangement"].apply(lambda a: f"{a[0]}-{a[1]}")
lat["slow"] = lat["fpog_first_fix_rt_ms"] > SLOW_MS

med = lat.groupby(["group", "arrangement_lbl"])["fpog_first_fix_rt_ms"].median().unstack(0)
pslow = lat.groupby(["group", "arrangement_lbl"])["slow"].mean().unstack(0)
```

Median latency for both groups (`med` above) stays between 248 and 285 ms across every arrangement and is not shown here, since the fast mode dominates almost everywhere and the group difference lives in the slow tail (`pslow`) instead.

![Share of first fixations slower than 2000 ms, by arrangement and group.](../images/results/latency_by_arrangement_fpog.png){#fig-latency width="85%"}

The slow tail concentrates in the three arrangements without an upper-left stimulus (7-1, 8-2, 12-6) for both groups, and in all three it is larger for RTL than for LTR: 7.6% against 5.7% in 7-1, 7.6% against 6.8% in 8-2, and 10.1% against 8.1% in 12-6. The other three arrangements offer an upper-left target and the tail nearly vanishes, reaching exactly 0% for both groups in 11-5 and for RTL in 10-4. So the same pattern that shows up in which stimulus was chosen also shows up in how long the choice took: RTL is slowest precisely where its preferred upper-left target is missing. These are raw shares with no confidence intervals, and each RTL cell holds 78 to 80 trials, so they carry the same caveat about sample size as the proportions do.
